topics.title: Introducing CKBSwap — Building on CKB for the Long Term

recent_posts.topic_title: Introducing CKBSwap — Building on CKB for the Long Term
recent_posts.author: asondev
recent_posts.content_text:
Hello, CKB community!
We are FoundationLab, a team of three developers who share a strong belief in CKB and a commitment to building within its ecosystem.
Today, we’d like to introduce CKBSwap, the project we’re working on.
Our goal is straightforward: build a useful, accessible swap and liquidity application that helps turn CKB’s technical potential into something people can use.
What is CKBSwap?
CKBSwap is an exchange and liquidity application built around CKB’s native asset model. It is currently on testnet.
It supports native CKB/xUDT and xUDT/xUDT liquidity pools using constant-product pricing. Users can swap assets, provide liquidity, and withdraw their share of the underlying assets. Liquidity providers receive standard xUDT LP tokens, while a 0.3% trading fee stays in the pool.
The interface follows a clear flow: select your assets, enter an amount, review the quote and slippage, preview the transaction, and sign through your connected wallet. Private keys remain with the wallet, and CKBSwap charges no additional frontend fee.
We see testnet as the beginning of a continuous process of testing, learning, and improvement. Community feedback will help us make each step clearer and more reliable.
Why we chose CKB
The more we learn about CKB, the more we appreciate the thought behind its architecture.
The Cell Model extends UTXO into a flexible foundation for programmable assets and state. Its treatment of ownership and validation gives developers room to rethink how applications can be built around assets that users control.
The RISC-V-based CKB-VM is equally compelling. Building on an open, general-purpose instruction set leaves room for different cryptographic schemes and verification logic to evolve. To us, that is a thoughtful engineering choice with a long horizon.
What stands out is how these decisions fit together. The Cell Model, CKB-VM, and layered architecture reflect a coherent vision for security, flexibility, and lasting utility. We find that combination elegant—and worth committing our time to.
Three people, committed to building
FoundationLab is a small team. All three of us want to contribute through practical work: improving the product, fixing problems, listening to users, and sharing progress the community can evaluate.
Our conviction in CKB comes with a responsibility to build. Strong infrastructure becomes more valuable when developers turn its capabilities into applications people choose to use. We want to play our part in that process.
CKBSwap is our starting point. We intend to keep learning, keep shipping, and grow alongside the CKB community.
We invite you to explore the testnet, share your feedback, and help us improve.
FoundationLab — three builders, starting with CKBSwap, committed to CKB for the long term.
Explore the project: ckbswap.site

recent_posts.content_text: 太棒了！去年我尝试过一个有些简陋的 bonding curve cell 的demo，现在看到有团队在实现类似的想法、但是是作为真正的消费级产品来做，真的太让人激动了 如果能提供更多关于 CKBSwap 的协议原理会对理解你们在做的产品有更大的帮助。比如，我个人会比较感兴趣的问题是，CKBSwap 是用什么原理在 utxo 架构上去做这种 pool 的？是否会有 hot cell 热更新的问题（比如许多人在同一个 pool 中去做swap，这里的并发是怎么处理的）？

recent_posts.topic_title: Introducing CKBSwap — Building on CKB for the Long Term
recent_posts.author: asondev
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks for the encouragement! We’d love to see your bonding-curve cell demo as well. You’re right—a clearer explanation of the protocol would make this introduction much more useful.
CKBSwap currently uses a constant-product AMM, following the familiar Uniswap V2 pricing model, implemented as a state machine over CKB Cells.
How the pool works
Each pool has a state cell recording its asset identifiers, reserves, total LP supply, and a nonce. For a CKB/xUDT pool, the CKB reserve is held directly in the state cell’s capacity, alongside its fixed storage allocation. Each xUDT reserve is held in a separate reserve cell tied to that pool.
A swap consumes the current pool state and reserve cells and creates their successors with updated balances. The on-chain script validates the transition, including the swap calculation, the fee-adjusted constant-product invariant, the user’s asset balance changes, and the specified slippage limits.
The 0.3% trading fee remains in the pool. Liquidity additions and withdrawals follow the same consume-and-recreate pattern, with corresponding LP minting or burning.
The hot cell issue
Yes, contention exists in the current design. If multiple users build swaps against the same pool state, their transactions compete for the same inputs. Once one transaction consumes those cells, the others need to be rebuilt against the updated state, with refreshed quotes and signing as needed.
We’re considering several improvements:
Per-pool queuing to coordinate transaction construction and reduce conflicting submissions.
Chained transactions to build on the outputs of pending transactions, reducing the need to wait for each swap to confirm before submitting the next.
Batch settlement, potentially through an intent-based design, to process multiple user orders within a single pool state transition.
These are directions we’re evaluating, not features already implemented. Queuing and chaining would help coordinate sequential updates, while batch settlement would require changes to the protocol and authorization model.
The contracts and protocol documentation are public here. We’re still on testnet, and feedback on these tradeoffs is very welcome.
Thanks for raising exactly the kind of technical discussion we hoped to have!

topics.title: Spark Program | NNCBN - Nervos Network Community Boot Nodes

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | NNCBN - Nervos Network Community Boot Nodes
recent_posts.author: NNCBN
recent_posts.content_text:
2026 October 27, Fifth Weekly Report
We have been operating the node for the first synchronization since the last weekly report till today! Some fine-tuning is still needed, but the synchronization is already complete, and after about a week of operation, the system has already proven that it has sufficient performance reserves and is running stably.
The next major step is to begin operations at the designated location. If all goes well, the next weekly report will announce that the node has been deployed and connected in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Africa, between Brazil and Portugal. We’re keeping our fingers crossed that everything goes smoothly.
Initial LOG-Sort tests.
Continued social media activity.

CKB Ecosystem Biweekly Update #27

image690×388 97.6 KB

Welcome to the latest CKB Ecosystem Biweekly Update. Here’s a quick summary of key dev and ecosystem progress from the past two weeks.

Infrastructure & Tooling

  • @CKBdev continued preparing CKB v0.211. CKB-VM and Tentacle gained runtime and networking improvements, while ckb-cli added a terminal UI. Light-client verification proposals remain under review, and experimental DAO voting progressed on vote thresholds and proposal settlement. More: CKB Dev Log 2026-10-14
  • @CKBDevrel made ckb-cinnabar easier for AI agents to discover and use, continued CCC development, and maintained CKBadger v0.7 services for mainnet and testnet.
  • @FiberDevs progressed toward Fiber v0.10, including invoice-settlement fixes. Channel V2 and Hosted LSP work continues on signing, recovery, and payment flows. More: Fiber Dev Log 2026-10-15

Web5 & DAO

  • @Code3ks is applying $6,000 from CKB Community Fund DAO for a 12-week development and validation phase for FiberNuts, an open Cashu-over-Fiber settlement adapter with RUSD reference applications. This proposal is now in the Discussion Stage.
  • @OWK50GA is applying $5,000 to advance CKB IDL. This proposal is now in the Discussion Stage.
  • @asondev is applying $20,000 to build CKB Poker, an online Texas Hold’em game with reusable multiplayer components. This proposal is now in the Discussion Stage.
  • @Ayoub_Lesfer is applying $5,000 for CrowdCell, a testnet-first, all-or-nothing crowdfunding app. This proposal has passed the Discussion Stage, and vote is live on Metaforo. Vote here.
  • @SalmanDev’s Kirea Finance proposal seeks $7,250 to harden native RWA lending primitives on CKB. It has passed the Discussion Stage, and vote is live on Metaforo. Vote here.
  • Rivet Phase 1 proposal by @Jedi_dtechmaker has passed DAO voting with 52.82% Yes.
  • Kaze × CKB UniTour Continuation proposal by @Dorex45 has passed DAO voting with 100% Yes.
  • @Jnr6 published Pocket Node for iOS Milestone 2 report, and released Pocket Node v1.8.6 (Android), providing better wallet protection and making backup and recovery easier to understand.
  • @Rypto posted the Month 2 report for the CKB Content Advocacy Campaign.
  • @truthixify published Vellum Milestone 2 delivery report.
  • @Ticoworld shared a FiberLatch Access post-grant update, demonstrating FiberFlow integration and local Fiber testnet settlement.
  • @Lawliet_Chan shared a weekly update: updated the design and feature development of Proof of Buy consensus.

Ecosystem Projects & Community

  • CKCon 2026 brought core developers and community contributors together in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia (Oct 12–16) to reconnect, share progress and ideas, and discuss what’s next for CKB.
  • A CCC paper by @zz_tovarishch and @Hanssen was accepted as a poster at IEEE ICDLT 2026, Dec 3–4 in Alcobaça, Portugal. Read the three design lessons from CCC to learn moe.
  • A Reddit AMA with Hanssen, CKBA’s DevRel team lead, concluded on Oct 9th. Read the answers if you missed it.
  • @Nervapes CAMP is live at nervape.com/pages/camp with ten artists and ten cities.
  • @ArthurZhang published the CellScript roadmap, introduced the experimental Tactus O1 based-rollup concept, proposed Project Matchmaker for brainstorming, and launched UTXOPlay in alpha.
  • @Victor_Okenwa published ckb-connect-wallet-kit, shared a wallet UI customization guide, and introduced Nervlith (formerly Mint Gate).
  • @LusoCryptoLabs launched POI: Proof of Identity, a testnet platformer teaching .cell names, and invited testers for the Cellula Wallet testnet beta.
  • @T_Silva introduced CKB Pulse, a live view of public CKB development on GitHub.
  • @TranNhi27 introduced FiberSurvivors, a browser-based, survivors-style game built around Fiber.
  • @Lawliet_Chan added notes on L1 censorship resistance to the Proof of Buy consensus.
  • @Mannychino published Understanding ‘Since’ on Nervos CKB.
  • @guopeng_lin released CKB Contract Flow, with visual Cell-transition explainers and an on-chain tx decoder for 46 CKB contracts.
  • @RetricSu released CKB On-ramp, a non-custodial first-deposit flow.

Nervos Community Catalyst & Spark Program

Nervos Community Catalyst

  • Nervos Community Catalyst released its Q3 2026 report: nearly 100 CKBuilders and alumni, 18 projects submitted for review, and 66 submissions from roughly 100 participants in the Fiber Infrastructure Hackathon. CKB Off-Chain expanded across regions, while CKBoost reached around 150 users.
  • Nervos Community Catalyst, in collaboration with BPSClub and TexLabs, held CKB Off-Chain Hanoi in Vietnam on Oct 8, 2026. Read the event recap.
  • CKB Builders Workshop in Kisumu, Kenya was concluded on Oct 16, 2026 with 37 people attending the event. Read the event recap.
  • Build on CKB: Campaign #7 is live. Send your first multi-hop payment with Fiber and win awards here.
  • The Vellum Test Campaign is running to test its portable quest-claim integration, with a listed end date of Nov 24. Join here.
  • @usekaze Kaze announced CKB-USDT and CKB-USDC swap support.
  • @blackbox_pos shared Devlog #10, showcasing prepaid-card and tap-to-pay functionality at the demo stage.
  • @xiaomao updated noir-ckb-verifier and opened participation in the private-tally trusted-setup ceremony.
  • @truthixify posted a post-hackathon update on Fiber Forge and released v0.4.0.
  • @karasbuilder introduced Nine Cells, a browser-based tower-defense game on testnet.
  • @Ticoworld introduced QuotaCell, a CKB-based treasury-spending tool, and Waymark Lite, a CKB wallet-state recovery tool, was integrated into Pocket Node’s main branch on Android and iOS.
  • @Code3ks shared fixes to FiberNuts Community Market, a Cashu + Fiber testnet app.
  • @ebubedev introduced Twine, an early, testnet-only P2P CKB/fiat trading prototype using Fiber and Nostr.
  • @Dat_Nguyen_Tu shared progress on CellRoute/FiberPay, a CKB developer-tooling and live asset-inspection project.
  • @LucentLabs shared CKB DEX progress update.
  • A new CKBuilder article in the Knowledge Base:
    • *CKBuilders: A new generation of blockchain creatives on CKB — Volume 2*
  • New Catalyst projects:
    • FiberContinuity: Browser-first backup and recovery reference for self-custodial Fiber apps.
    • FreightOnNervos (FON): A CKB-native deliverables network.
    • CKAutomata: Payment automation and Nervos DAO harvesting.
    • Crowns: A multiplayer skill game with runs replayable on CKB-VM.

Spark Program

  • The Spark Committee approved the final evaluation of Wallet Behaviour Intelligence project.
  • Regular updates from approved projects:
    • NNCBN
    • Tranfr
    • CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint
    • Seedsong
  • New or pending applications:
    • Corven: Browser-based IDE for CKB and Fiber.
    • create-ckb-passkey-app: CKB passkey-auth starter kit.
    • MeterNet: Pay-per-MB Wi-Fi hotspots using Fiber.
    • Spark Verify: Reproducible acceptance checks for CKB projects.
    • Bees Network: Decentralized observation layer for AI agents.
    • DAO Cycle Alerts: Telegram reminders for Nervos DAO cycles.
    • MatchLock: Private-until-match bilateral settlement primitive.
  • Rejected applications:
    • LiquidLane: Fiber receive-capacity marketplace (resubmission).
    • Fiber Mystery Shopper: Independent paid-use testing of Fiber services.
    • RGB++ Resume: Recovery of interrupted RGB++ transfers.

Every step forward in CKB is powered by the community. Let’s keep building!

Thanks to @JackyLHH for his contribution to the edition of the bi-weekly update.
